newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nissan Motor joins long list of yen beneficiaries.
newsitem.headline: Nissan Motor joins long list of yen beneficiaries.

text.p: Nissan Motor Co Ltd on Tuesday joined the list of Japanese car giants which have posted windfall profits from the weaker yen, saying its parent company profit more than doubled in the last business year.

The brisk earnings by car makers helped buoy Japan Inc's overall profit by more than ten percent in the year which ended in March, but analysts warned that the fate of the sector's business still hinges on currencies.

"It's all up to currencies," said Koji Endo, a senior vice president of Lehman Brothers Japan Inc. "A dollar rate of 110 yen is seen as break even. If the dollar gets weaker than that, automakers would suffer slower profit growth this year."

Japanese car makers have actively shifted production bases abroad, although they still need to raise exports in order to meet soaring overseas demand especially from Americans. The increased production overseas also increased their exports of car parts to the region, analysts said.
Their solid exports may offset a likely drop in domestic sales resulting from Japan's sales tax rise in April, while fuelling fears over another trade row with the United States.

"There is no change in the automakers' structure which is vulnerable to currency swings," Endo said. They would suffer losses if the yen strengthened to 70 yen to the dollar, but their profits will jump if it weakens to 120, he said.

Nissan, the nation's second biggest automaker, announced that parent current profits totalled 81.03 billion yen ($698 million) in 1996/97, 2.5 times as much as in the previous year, as the weak yen made its products more competitive abroad.
Nissan also zoomed back into profit on a group basis, landing in the black for the first time in five years.

Its group net profit hit 77.74 billion yen ($670 million) in 1996/97 after the previous year's loss of 88.42 billion yen ($762 million). Net profit is equal to current profit, which is pre-tax, minus taxes and extraordinary profits and losses.
Annual profits at other car giants like Toyota Motor Corp and Honda Motor Co Ltd had soared to record levels, as they also reaped the benefit of the weak yen.
Last week, Toyota said group net profit enjoyed a hefty rise of over 50 percent to 385.92 billion yen ($3.32 billion), with its parent-only profit growing 80 percent to a record.
Honda's group net profit also more than tripled in 1996/97 to a record 221.17 billion yen ($1.90 billion).

"The robust profit in the car sector contributed to Japan's overall corporate profit growth of over ten percent last business year" since the sector has a heavy spillover effect on other businesses like steel and electronics, said Hiroki Matsushita, analyst at Wako Research Institute of Economics.

But Japanese car makers, including Nissan, have predicted their profit growth would be less dramatic this year, using calculations based on a dollar rate of around 110-115 yen, largely identical to last year's.
The yen averaged around 113 yen to the dollar during the last business year, about 15 percent lower than the year before. On Tuesday, it stood at about 116 to the dollar in late afternoon Tokyo.
Nissan saw a rise of about 36 percent in its parent-only profit and said it was aiming for a group net profit of more than 100 billion yen ($862 million) for this year.

"Nissan expected its Mexican operation to break even in 1997/98, while its European unit, which was in the red during the last business year, was also expected to break even this year," a Nissan director Kanemitsu Anraku told reporters.

Still, Nissan was among the "losers" in the car sector with another troubled automaker Mazda Motor Corp, which said last week that its group profit would remain in the red in 1996/97 for a fourth successive year.

Their weaker positions are well reflected in share prices. Nissan and Mazda ended the Tuesday session in Tokyo at 739 yen ($6) and 348 ($3) yen respectively, much lower than Toyota and Honda, which ended the day at 3,510 yen ($30) and 3,540 yen ($30) respectively.
"The order will not change for now," said Lehman Brothers' Endo. But he added some buying may emerge for Nissan and Mazda if their business proved to be on a clear recovery track. ($1=116 yen)
